headline: There's a protein
body: And unlike most findings in this field, it comes with human genetic evidence.
punch: Most growth-plate results never get that far.

headline: Osteolectin
body: As a factor maintaining adult bone mass. That was its whole described job — keeping an existing skeleton dense.

headline: In young animals
body: Osteolectin increases growth plate chondrocyte proliferation and promotes bone elongation, producing increased body length in juvenile mice.
punch: A different function in a different life stage.

headline: Which is a pattern
body: The same molecule doing maintenance in adults and construction in juveniles. Growth biology and maintenance biology reuse the same parts for different jobs.
punch: Ask what a protein does at your age, not in general.

headline: Then the rare part
body: A human genetic variant in osteolectin was identified and linked to a functional phenotype — direct human genetic evidence, not mouse-model inference.
punch: Almost nothing else in this literature clears that bar.

headline: Why that matters
body: Mouse growth-plate findings frequently fail to transfer — rodents don't undergo true epiphyseal fusion at sexual maturity the way humans do.
punch: A human variant sidesteps the species problem entirely.

headline: What it doesn't mean
body: There is no osteolectin intervention. This is a mechanism with unusually good evidence, not an available lever, and the gap between those is enormous.

headline: The real lesson
body: When you hear a growth claim, ask whether it rests on a mouse, a cell culture, or a human genetic variant. Those aren't the same kind of knowing.
punch: The species the finding lives in tells you most of what you need.

headline: It's never over
body: Real mechanisms, real citations, no protocols.
